newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil dollar flows cover current account gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil dollar flows cover current account gap.

text.p: Dollar inflows into Brazil are continuing at a high rate in October, signalling easy financing of the current account gap, the Finance Ministry said on Thursday.
The ministry said in its monthly report on economic indicators that the proportion of the inflows consisting of short-term speculative capital was decreasing.
"Even with a fall we have seen in the exchange rate coupon (domestic interest rates minus exchange rate fluctuations) the inflow of capital...continues at a high level," it said.
"This, together with the growing inflow of direct investment (FDI), signals a favourable outlook for financing the current account deficit," it added.
The ministry's monthly bulletin does not necessarily reflect official views and is based on private sector forecasts.

It said up to October 18, dollar inflows showed a $1.578 billion surplus versus a $875 million surplus in all of September. It said that despite a drop in the dollar coupon, the Central Bank's foreign reserves had not dipped noticeably and that this indicated short-term speculative capital outflows were more than offset by inflows via loans or direct investment.
"(This) shows that we are experiencing a change in the composition of capital inflows, with long-term capital increasing in proportion," the ministry said.

It said FDI of $5.8 billion up to end-September covered more than 40 percent of the current account gap, which according to a new method of calculating gross domestic product reached 2.53 percent of GDP in the first nine months.

The ministry noted that Brazil's external accounts, pressured recently by poorer-than-expected trade figures, fared well when compared with projections by international banks for some Asian countries usually held up as role models.

It said Indonesia was expected to run a current account gap of 3.7 percent of GDP in 1996, Malaysia 9.7 percent of GDP and Thailand 7.7 percent of GDP against official projections for Brazil of a 2.5 percent of GDP current account deficit.

After taking account of FDI, Indonesia would run a gap of 1.8 percent of GDP, Malaysia 3.8 percent of GDP and Thailand 7.5 percent of GDP, it said, while Brazil's external accounts financing needs would be about 1.4 percent of GDP.
